story_ideas.title: Statutorily Mandated Designation of Difficult Development Areas and Qualified Census Tracts for 2027
story_ideas.headline: HUD just redrew the map of where affordable senior apartments pencil out
story_ideas.angle: A read of HUD's 2027 Difficult Development Area and Qualified Census Tract designations for what they change about Low-Income Housing Tax Credit math in the places older renters actually live, written for developers and for renters on a waiting list.
story_ideas.hook: HUD makes these designations annually and the 2027 list published 10/06/26, resetting which locations carry the credit advantage before next year's allocation rounds.
story_ideas.summary: This document designates "Difficult Development Areas" (DDAs) and "Qualified Census Tracts" (QCTs) for purposes of the Low- Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC). The United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) makes new DDA and QCT designations annually.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are waiting on an income-restricted apartment, look up whether your census tract made HUD's 2027 list, because that designation is a large part of why a builder does or does not choose your neighborhood.
story_ideas.b2b: Which markets gained and lost designation going into 2027, and what that does to underwriting on senior affordable deals already in predevelopment.
story_ideas.chart: The underlying file supports an original ranking or trend line.
story_ideas.competitive: Monitored trades cover this beat and have not written it.
story_ideas.why: A tract's designation sits upstream of whether any affordable unit gets built near you, and nobody will tell you it changed.
story_ideas.note: Localizable to states and tracts; monitored publishers cover this beat and none matched the item.

story_ideas.title: Notice of HUD-Held Healthcare Loan Sale (HLS 2027-1)
story_ideas.headline: Eleven healthcare mortgages go to auction in November with no federal insurance attached
story_ideas.angle: A short piece tracking HUD's competitive sealed bid sale of 11 unsubsidized healthcare mortgage loans, scheduled on or about 11/17/26, for the capital markets readers who bid and the families whose buildings carry the paper.
story_ideas.hook: HUD is selling defaulted healthcare assets without FHA insurance, which changes who holds the mortgage on a care property and on what terms.
story_ideas.consumer: If a parent lives in a facility you believe is financially strained, ask the administrator directly whether its mortgage is federally held, and what a change of lender would mean for staffing and services.
story_ideas.b2b: The pricing on HLS 2027-1 is a live read on what distressed healthcare paper is worth right now, and on how aggressively HUD is clearing held assets.
story_ideas.why: A lender change rarely reaches residents as news, but it often precedes a change in who runs the building.
story_ideas.note: Sale date on or about 11/17/26; confirmed gap among monitored publishers.

story_ideas.title: Current and Historical Public Opinion on Medicare-for-All and Other National Health Plan Proposals
story_ideas.headline: Two-thirds now back Medicare-for-all, and the number moves the moment anyone argues
story_ideas.angle: A piece on KFF's updated chart pack showing a new polling high for Medicare-for-all alongside how sharply support shifts once respondents hear proponents and critics, for readers who will be hearing exactly those arguments through November.
story_ideas.hook: The headline figure is a record in KFF's own polling series, and the same chart pack shows how unstable it is under argument.
story_ideas.consumer: When a candidate quotes a poll number at you this month, check whether it is the raw figure or the one measured after people heard the counterargument.
story_ideas.b2b: Payers and provider groups preparing midterm messaging now have a documented measure of how much movement a single framing buys.
story_ideas.why: Knowing a number is soft protects you from being told it is a mandate.
story_ideas.note: Published 10/06/26; chartable time series; confirmed gap.

story_ideas.title: A Look at Waiting Lists for Medicaid Home- and Community-Based Services from 2016 to 2026
story_ideas.headline: Your state's home care waiting list will not tell you how long you will wait
story_ideas.angle: A plain-language explainer of KFF's 2016 to 2026 waiting list data note, which says outright that lists are an incomplete measure of unmet need and are not comparable across states, for families being told to get on one.
story_ideas.hook: The organization that collects the numbers is warning against the way the numbers are used.
story_ideas.summary: Oct 5, 2026 Issue Brief This data note provides new information about waiting lists from KFF’s most recent survey of state Medicaid home care programs, including a discussion of why waiting lists are an incomplete measure of unmet need and why they are not necessarily comparable across states or over time, despite KFF’s efforts to obtain as consistent data as possible.
story_ideas.consumer: Ask your state Medicaid agency what its list actually screens for and who gets removed, because the length of the list is not the length of your wait.
story_ideas.b2b: Home care operators and state agencies are being measured on a metric the source describes as inconsistent, which matters for anyone citing it in a budget request.
story_ideas.chart: The figures in the finding are the spine of a simple graphic.
story_ideas.competitive: Monitored trades cover this beat and have not written it.
story_ideas.why: A family that reads the list as a queue plans for a date that was never real.
story_ideas.note: Published 10/05/26; state-level cuts available; confirmed gap.

story_ideas.title: States' Use of Program Integrity Tools in Medicaid Home Care
story_ideas.headline: The checks your state runs on the aide who comes to your door
story_ideas.angle: A survey-based look at which program integrity tools state Medicaid home care programs are using, written for the person whose authorized hours get verified and the agency that has to document them.
story_ideas.hook: KFF's newest state survey puts numbers on oversight practices that usually only surface when a payment is denied.
story_ideas.consumer: If your aide's hours were cut or questioned, ask your state program which verification requirement triggered it and what documentation fixes it.
story_ideas.b2b: Compliance load varies by state, and this is the first clean comparison of what home care agencies are being asked to prove.
story_ideas.why: An hour denied for a paperwork reason is still an hour of care you did not get.
story_ideas.note: Published 10/05/26; light coverage among monitored publishers rather than a full gap.

story_ideas.title: Global Benchmark for Efficient Drug Pricing (GLOBE) Model
story_ideas.headline: Medicare is about to calculate Part B drug rebates a different way, and participation is mandatory
story_ideas.angle: A walkthrough of the final rule implementing the GLOBE Model, which tests an alternative method for calculating Part B drug inflation rebate amounts, for readers whose infusions and injections are billed under Part B.
story_ideas.hook: This is a mandatory Medicare payment model created under section 1115A of the Social Security Act, not a voluntary demonstration providers can opt out of.
story_ideas.consumer: If a drug you receive in a clinic is billed to Part B, ask the practice whether it falls under the new model and whether your coinsurance changes.
story_ideas.b2b: Practices and infusion providers need to know which separately payable Part B drugs are in scope before the model's payment math reaches their remittances.
story_ideas.why: Part B coinsurance is a percentage, so a change in how the benchmark is set reaches your out-of-pocket cost directly.

story_ideas.title: How Much Do Older Workers Value Retiree Health Insurance?
story_ideas.headline: The benefit older workers will not quit a job to lose
story_ideas.angle: A piece on new Center for Retirement Research work valuing retiree health insurance to older workers, set beside BLS data showing employment of people 65 and over at 11,654 thousand in September 2026, down 0.7% year over year.
story_ideas.hook: The research puts a value on the single benefit most often cited as the reason people keep working past 65, in a month when the 65-plus employment count fell.
story_ideas.consumer: Before you take a retirement date, price what replacing employer retiree coverage would cost you, and treat that figure as part of your compensation.
story_ideas.b2b: Employers using retention incentives for experienced staff have a reason to look at coverage design rather than pay alone.
story_ideas.why: Retiree coverage is the quietest line in a retirement decision and the most expensive one to get wrong.
story_ideas.note: Published 10/06/26; no monitored publisher is watching this beat, so coverage status is unknown rather than clear.

story_ideas.headline: Where the 65-and-over population actually lives, counted state by state
story_ideas.angle: A data piece built on the 2023 ACS five-year estimates, which put 5,994,486 residents aged 65 and over in California and 4,630,733 in Florida, with 65-74, 75-84 and 85-plus breakouts plus median household income and housing tenure, for anyone siting services or comparing states.
story_ideas.hook: The 85-plus breakout and housing tenure in the same table is what turns a population count into a care-demand estimate.
story_ideas.summary: State-level counts for 65+, 65-74, 75-84 and 85+ populations with median household income and housing tenure, 2023 ACS 5-year estimates.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are weighing a move, compare your target state's 75-84 and 85-plus counts and median household income rather than its reputation as a retirement destination.

story_ideas.competitive: Monitored trades cover this beat and have not written it.
story_ideas.why: State choice sets your cost of care and your neighbors' ability to pay for it, and both are in this one table.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Medical Equipment Suppliers
story_ideas.headline: Look up which equipment suppliers near you take Medicare before you need a wheelchair
story_ideas.angle: A service piece on the refreshed CMS supplier file, which lists what each location carries and its Medicare participation status, for anyone arranging equipment after a fall or a discharge.
story_ideas.hook: Participation status is the difference between a billed claim and a bill you pay, and it is searchable by state and county.
story_ideas.summary: A list of Suppliers that indicates the supplies carried at that location and the supplier's Medicare participation status.
story_ideas.consumer: Check a supplier's Medicare participation status in the CMS file before you accept a delivery, and ask what the same item costs if the supplier does not participate.
story_ideas.b2b: Referral sources sending discharges to non-participating suppliers create downstream billing disputes that land back on the discharging provider.
story_ideas.localize: Breaks down to US states, US counties — rank the outliers.
story_ideas.competitive: Reference data — a refreshed file, so no coverage claim applies either way.
story_ideas.why: The wrong supplier turns a covered item into an out-of-pocket purchase.
story_ideas.note: This is a refreshed public data file dated 10/04/26, not an event; the value is in the lookup, not the update.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Unplanned Hospital Visits - Hospital
story_ideas.headline: Before a discharge, check how often that hospital's patients come back
story_ideas.angle: A how-to on the CMS unplanned hospital visits file, which carries excess days in acute care, unplanned readmission measures and unplanned visits after outpatient procedures, for families managing a transition to rehab or home.
story_ideas.hook: Readmission and return-day measures are published at the provider level and almost never consulted before the decision they should inform.
story_ideas.consumer: Pull the readmission measures for the hospital discharging your parent and ask the discharge planner what follow-up is arranged in the first 30 days.
story_ideas.b2b: Skilled nursing operators negotiating referral relationships can show hospital partners where return days concentrate and who absorbs them.
story_ideas.why: A readmission costs an older adult a second hospitalization, which is the single event most likely to end independent living.
story_ideas.note: Refreshed file dated 09/10/26, state and county cuts available; use it as a tool, not as news.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Home health care services average hourly earnings, August 2026 — 28.14 dollars per hour (+2.4% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: What 28 dollars an hour buys the family hiring an aide
story_ideas.angle: A cost piece pricing home care against the August 2026 BLS average hourly earnings figure of 28.14 dollars, up 2.4% year over year, for families budgeting hours rather than reading payroll data.
story_ideas.hook: Sector wage growth of 2.4% sits above the medical care CPI's 1.6% year-over-year rise for the same month, which is unusual for a labor line in this field.
story_ideas.consumer: Translate the hourly figure into a weekly budget before you commit to a care schedule, and ask any agency how its rate compares to the sector average.
story_ideas.b2b: Agencies competing for the same workers can see whether their pay scale clears the national average in a month when sector pay outpaced medical prices.
story_ideas.why: Hours are the unit families actually buy, and an hourly figure is what tells you how many you can afford.

story_ideas.title: Medicare Program; FY 2027 Hospice Wage Index and Payment Rate Update and Hospice Quality Reporting Program Requirements; Correction
story_ideas.headline: The hospice payment rule for fiscal 2027 got corrected, and providers should read the fix
story_ideas.angle: A short regulatory read on the correction to technical errors in the FY 2027 hospice wage index final rule originally published 08/03/26, for hospice finance staff and for families comparing providers.
story_ideas.hook: Wage index corrections change payment by region, which is why a technical notice is not a technical matter for a small hospice.
story_ideas.consumer: Hospice is a Medicare benefit with no bill at the point of care, so what changes here is which providers can afford to staff your area, not what you pay.
story_ideas.b2b: Nonprofit and rural hospices operating on thin margins need to confirm whether the corrected figures alter their fiscal 2027 assumptions.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** The 2025 reconciliation law's Medicaid provisions now have a state-by-state map, and it landed in the week polling put health costs at the top of the midterm ballot. KFF published "Which States Will Be Affected by Key Medicaid Provisions in the 2025 Reconciliation Law?" on 10/07/26, sorting states by exposure to new work requirements, immigrant eligibility restrictions, and changes to provider taxes and state directed payments. On 10/06/26 KFF's Health Tracking Poll found health care costs tied with gas as voters' top midterm concern, and a companion chart pack put support for Medicare-for-all at two-thirds of the public, a new high that moves sharply once respondents hear arguments on either side. Read together, those three make it possible to say which states are about to change the financing of the program that pays for home care and nursing home care, and to set that against what voters in those states say they are voting on. The wider Medicare and Medicaid cluster, 36 items from 9 sources, shares a tag rather than a subject and should not be worked as one story.

**Why it matters:** Medicaid is the payer behind most long-term services and supports, and the brief says every state is touched through eligibility and financing changes. The financing provisions are the quiet ones: a change to provider taxes or state directed payments reaches a home care program without ever appearing in a beneficiary's mail. KFF's own data note on home- and community-based services waiting lists, 2016 to 2026, says plainly that waiting lists are an incomplete measure of unmet need and are not comparable across states, so the people who lose access first are the hardest to count. For scale, the 2023 American Community Survey puts 5,994,486 residents aged 65 and over in California and 4,630,733 in Florida. What a family gains from this piece is the ability to name the specific provision their own state is applying, rather than reading a national number that describes nobody's program.

**Why pitch this now:** The brief is dated 10/07/26 and the KFF poll says the midterms are about a month away. State decisions on provider taxes and directed payments are being made against that calendar, and the window where a reader can connect a ballot to a benefit closes in early November.

**Angle:** Can an older adult on Medicaid find out, before they vote, which provisions of the 2025 law their own state is about to apply to the program that pays for their care, and which states are quietly changing financing rather than eligibility? Working title: "Fifty Medicaid Programs, One Law." For state health policy readers and for families managing a parent's long-term care coverage.

**Potential headlines:**
- Your state is about to apply the 2025 Medicaid law its own way
- Health care costs tied with gas at the top of the midterm ballot
- The Medicaid changes nobody will mail you a notice about

**Potential outlets:**
- **Modern Healthcare** — covers Medicaid financing mechanics such as provider taxes and state directed payments as business news, which is where the under-reported half of this law sits.
- **Fierce Healthcare** — payer and policy readers tracking how states operationalize eligibility restrictions, with the midterm polling as the political frame.
- **SeniorLiving.org** — a consumer senior-living audience that needs the state-level version of this, not the national one.
- **Bankrate Retirement** — readers planning around long-term care costs who need to know that Medicaid's terms are being reset state by state.
pitch_draft_raw: KFF's 10/07/26 issue brief finally makes the 2025 reconciliation law legible one state at a time: which states face the new work requirements, which face immigrant eligibility restrictions, and which are exposed through provider taxes and state directed payments. I want to write the financing half, because that is the half nobody gets a notice about. A state can leave eligibility rules alone and still shrink what its home care program buys. I would set that against KFF's 10/06/26 Health Tracking Poll, where health care costs tied with gas as voters' top midterm concern, and against KFF's data note on home- and community-based services waiting lists from 2016 to 2026, which says outright that those lists are an incomplete measure of unmet need and not comparable across states. About 1,200 words, built around a state table readers can find themselves in. Modern Healthcare's audience already follows directed payments as a business story; this is the version with a beneficiary at the end of it.
pitch_ideas_raw:
**HUD just redrew the map of where affordable senior apartments pencil out**
*Statutorily Mandated Designation of Difficult Development Areas and Qualified Census Tracts for 2027*  
- Angle: A read of HUD's 2027 Difficult Development Area and Qualified Census Tract designations for what they change about Low-Income Housing Tax Credit math in the places older renters actually live, written for developers and for renters on a waiting list.
- Hook: HUD makes these designations annually and the 2027 list published 10/06/26, resetting which locations carry the credit advantage before next year's allocation rounds.
- For readers: If you are waiting on an income-restricted apartment, look up whether your census tract made HUD's 2027 list, because that designation is a large part of why a builder does or does not choose your neighborhood.
- For the trade: Which markets gained and lost designation going into 2027, and what that does to underwriting on senior affordable deals already in predevelopment.
- Why it matters: A tract's designation sits upstream of whether any affordable unit gets built near you, and nobody will tell you it changed.
- Also: Localizable to states and tracts; monitored publishers cover this beat and none matched the item.
- Pitch to: Senior Housing News, Seniors Housing Business

**Eleven healthcare mortgages go to auction in November with no federal insurance attached**
*Notice of HUD-Held Healthcare Loan Sale (HLS 2027-1)*  
- Angle: A short piece tracking HUD's competitive sealed bid sale of 11 unsubsidized healthcare mortgage loans, scheduled on or about 11/17/26, for the capital markets readers who bid and the families whose buildings carry the paper.
- Hook: HUD is selling defaulted healthcare assets without FHA insurance, which changes who holds the mortgage on a care property and on what terms.
- For readers: If a parent lives in a facility you believe is financially strained, ask the administrator directly whether its mortgage is federally held, and what a change of lender would mean for staffing and services.
- For the trade: The pricing on HLS 2027-1 is a live read on what distressed healthcare paper is worth right now, and on how aggressively HUD is clearing held assets.
- Why it matters: A lender change rarely reaches residents as news, but it often precedes a change in who runs the building.
- Also: Sale date on or about 11/17/26; confirmed gap among monitored publishers.
- Pitch to: Seniors Housing Business, Senior Housing News

**Two-thirds now back Medicare-for-all, and the number moves the moment anyone argues**
*Current and Historical Public Opinion on Medicare-for-All and Other National Health Plan Proposals*  
- Angle: A piece on KFF's updated chart pack showing a new polling high for Medicare-for-all alongside how sharply support shifts once respondents hear proponents and critics, for readers who will be hearing exactly those arguments through November.
- Hook: The headline figure is a record in KFF's own polling series, and the same chart pack shows how unstable it is under argument.
- For readers: When a candidate quotes a poll number at you this month, check whether it is the raw figure or the one measured after people heard the counterargument.
- For the trade: Payers and provider groups preparing midterm messaging now have a documented measure of how much movement a single framing buys.
- Why it matters: Knowing a number is soft protects you from being told it is a mandate.
- Also: Published 10/06/26; chartable time series; confirmed gap.
- Pitch to: Modern Healthcare, Bankrate Retirement

**Your state's home care waiting list will not tell you how long you will wait**
*A Look at Waiting Lists for Medicaid Home- and Community-Based Services from 2016 to 2026*  
- Angle: A plain-language explainer of KFF's 2016 to 2026 waiting list data note, which says outright that lists are an incomplete measure of unmet need and are not comparable across states, for families being told to get on one.
- Hook: The organization that collects the numbers is warning against the way the numbers are used.
- For readers: Ask your state Medicaid agency what its list actually screens for and who gets removed, because the length of the list is not the length of your wait.
- For the trade: Home care operators and state agencies are being measured on a metric the source describes as inconsistent, which matters for anyone citing it in a budget request.
- Why it matters: A family that reads the list as a queue plans for a date that was never real.
- Also: Published 10/05/26; state-level cuts available; confirmed gap.
- Pitch to: SeniorLiving.org, Fierce Healthcare

**The checks your state runs on the aide who comes to your door**
*States' Use of Program Integrity Tools in Medicaid Home Care*  
- Angle: A survey-based look at which program integrity tools state Medicaid home care programs are using, written for the person whose authorized hours get verified and the agency that has to document them.
- Hook: KFF's newest state survey puts numbers on oversight practices that usually only surface when a payment is denied.
- For readers: If your aide's hours were cut or questioned, ask your state program which verification requirement triggered it and what documentation fixes it.
- For the trade: Compliance load varies by state, and this is the first clean comparison of what home care agencies are being asked to prove.
- Why it matters: An hour denied for a paperwork reason is still an hour of care you did not get.
- Also: Published 10/05/26; light coverage among monitored publishers rather than a full gap.
- Pitch to: Fierce Healthcare, SeniorLiving.org

**Medicare is about to calculate Part B drug rebates a different way, and participation is mandatory**
*Global Benchmark for Efficient Drug Pricing (GLOBE) Model*  
- Angle: A walkthrough of the final rule implementing the GLOBE Model, which tests an alternative method for calculating Part B drug inflation rebate amounts, for readers whose infusions and injections are billed under Part B.
- Hook: This is a mandatory Medicare payment model created under section 1115A of the Social Security Act, not a voluntary demonstration providers can opt out of.
- For readers: If a drug you receive in a clinic is billed to Part B, ask the practice whether it falls under the new model and whether your coinsurance changes.
- For the trade: Practices and infusion providers need to know which separately payable Part B drugs are in scope before the model's payment math reaches their remittances.
- Why it matters: Part B coinsurance is a percentage, so a change in how the benchmark is set reaches your out-of-pocket cost directly.
- Also: Final rule published 10/02/26; confirmed gap.
- Pitch to: ThinkAdvisor, Bankrate Retirement

**The benefit older workers will not quit a job to lose**
*How Much Do Older Workers Value Retiree Health Insurance?*  
- Angle: A piece on new Center for Retirement Research work valuing retiree health insurance to older workers, set beside BLS data showing employment of people 65 and over at 11,654 thousand in September 2026, down 0.7% year over year.
- Hook: The research puts a value on the single benefit most often cited as the reason people keep working past 65, in a month when the 65-plus employment count fell.
- For readers: Before you take a retirement date, price what replacing employer retiree coverage would cost you, and treat that figure as part of your compensation.
- For the trade: Employers using retention incentives for experienced staff have a reason to look at coverage design rather than pay alone.
- Why it matters: Retiree coverage is the quietest line in a retirement decision and the most expensive one to get wrong.
- Also: Published 10/06/26; no monitored publisher is watching this beat, so coverage status is unknown rather than clear.
- Pitch to: Next Avenue, GOBankingRates

**Where the 65-and-over population actually lives, counted state by state**
*American Community Survey 2023 state aging and housing profile (52 states)*  
- Angle: A data piece built on the 2023 ACS five-year estimates, which put 5,994,486 residents aged 65 and over in California and 4,630,733 in Florida, with 65-74, 75-84 and 85-plus breakouts plus median household income and housing tenure, for anyone siting services or comparing states.
- Hook: The 85-plus breakout and housing tenure in the same table is what turns a population count into a care-demand estimate.
- For readers: If you are weighing a move, compare your target state's 75-84 and 85-plus counts and median household income rather than its reputation as a retirement destination.
- For the trade: Tenure data alongside age bands gives developers a defensible read on owner-occupied equity available in each state's oldest cohort.
- Why it matters: State choice sets your cost of care and your neighbors' ability to pay for it, and both are in this one table.
- Also: 52-state file, directly chartable; confirmed gap and repeatedly cited in prior runs without ever carrying a story.
- Pitch to: Kiplinger, Senior Housing News

**Look up which equipment suppliers near you take Medicare before you need a wheelchair**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Medical Equipment Suppliers*  
- Angle: A service piece on the refreshed CMS supplier file, which lists what each location carries and its Medicare participation status, for anyone arranging equipment after a fall or a discharge.
- Hook: Participation status is the difference between a billed claim and a bill you pay, and it is searchable by state and county.
- For readers: Check a supplier's Medicare participation status in the CMS file before you accept a delivery, and ask what the same item costs if the supplier does not participate.
- For the trade: Referral sources sending discharges to non-participating suppliers create downstream billing disputes that land back on the discharging provider.
- Why it matters: The wrong supplier turns a covered item into an out-of-pocket purchase.
- Also: This is a refreshed public data file dated 10/04/26, not an event; the value is in the lookup, not the update.
- Pitch to: SeniorLiving.org, Bankrate Retirement

**Before a discharge, check how often that hospital's patients come back**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Unplanned Hospital Visits - Hospital*  
- Angle: A how-to on the CMS unplanned hospital visits file, which carries excess days in acute care, unplanned readmission measures and unplanned visits after outpatient procedures, for families managing a transition to rehab or home.
- Hook: Readmission and return-day measures are published at the provider level and almost never consulted before the decision they should inform.
- For readers: Pull the readmission measures for the hospital discharging your parent and ask the discharge planner what follow-up is arranged in the first 30 days.
- For the trade: Skilled nursing operators negotiating referral relationships can show hospital partners where return days concentrate and who absorbs them.
- Why it matters: A readmission costs an older adult a second hospitalization, which is the single event most likely to end independent living.
- Also: Refreshed file dated 09/10/26, state and county cuts available; use it as a tool, not as news.
- Pitch to: Skilled Nursing News, Family Caregiver Alliance

**What 28 dollars an hour buys the family hiring an aide**
*BLS: Home health care services average hourly earnings, August 2026 — 28.14 dollars per hour (+2.4% year over year)*  
- Angle: A cost piece pricing home care against the August 2026 BLS average hourly earnings figure of 28.14 dollars, up 2.4% year over year, for families budgeting hours rather than reading payroll data.
- Hook: Sector wage growth of 2.4% sits above the medical care CPI's 1.6% year-over-year rise for the same month, which is unusual for a labor line in this field.
- For readers: Translate the hourly figure into a weekly budget before you commit to a care schedule, and ask any agency how its rate compares to the sector average.
- For the trade: Agencies competing for the same workers can see whether their pay scale clears the national average in a month when sector pay outpaced medical prices.
- Why it matters: Hours are the unit families actually buy, and an hourly figure is what tells you how many you can afford.
- Also: Published 08/01/26; the September earnings print has not landed, so this is the current figure.
- Pitch to: Caring.com, Next Avenue

**The hospice payment rule for fiscal 2027 got corrected, and providers should read the fix**
*Medicare Program; FY 2027 Hospice Wage Index and Payment Rate Update and Hospice Quality Reporting Program Requirements; Correction*  
- Angle: A short regulatory read on the correction to technical errors in the FY 2027 hospice wage index final rule originally published 08/03/26, for hospice finance staff and for families comparing providers.
- Hook: Wage index corrections change payment by region, which is why a technical notice is not a technical matter for a small hospice.
- For readers: Hospice is a Medicare benefit with no bill at the point of care, so what changes here is which providers can afford to staff your area, not what you pay.
- For the trade: Nonprofit and rural hospices operating on thin margins need to confirm whether the corrected figures alter their fiscal 2027 assumptions.
- Why it matters: Payment geography decides which hospices still serve your county.
- Also: Correction published 09/30/26; confirmed gap among monitored publishers.
- Pitch to: LeadingAge, Fierce Healthcare
